NICO ROSBERG’S TWO DIFFERENT STANDARDS?

During Sky F1’s post-race coverage at Monza, Rosberg — who believed Leclerc was 100% responsible for forcing Hamilton off at Turn 2 — explained that Ferrari still couldn’t prioritise Lewis because Charles is the team’s “golden boy” and remains mathematically in the championship.

Interesting.

Because the same Nico Rosberg believes McLaren should eventually support Norris, whom he considers “clearly the best driver” in that team.

After Monza, Hamilton is 76 points behind Antonelli. Leclerc is another 36 points behind Lewis — meaning he is approximately 112 points away from the championship lead with 10 races remaining.

Mathematically possible? Yes.

Competitively realistic in a Ferrari that hasn’t consistently matched Mercedes since Silverstone? Absolutely not, in my opinion.

The most revealing part of Rosberg’s statement isn’t “mathematical chance”. It’s “golden boy”.

It suggests that Ferrari isn’t only considering the championship situation. The team is also managing Leclerc’s special status inside the organisation.

Was Rosberg trying to balance his earlier criticism of Charles? We cannot know. But Nico enjoys taking the opposite position, and he knows that every opinion he gives about Hamilton carries extra weight and generates reactions.

After all, he will always be introduced as the 2016 World Champion who “beat Lewis in equal machinery”.

Rosberg says Ferrari may have to “play the game” later.

Hamilton says it is already far too late.

That is the real problem: Ferrari waited so long to make a decision that there may now be nothing left to decide.

Sporting fairness — or a convenient double standard?

Source: Sky Sports F1 / Crash.net

#F1 #NicoRosberg #LewisHamilton #CharlesLeclerc #Ferrari #ScuderiaFerrari #ItalianGP

Nico Rosberg found an easy target after F1’s first race at the Madring: Carlos Sainz.

With the Spanish driver acting as an ambassador for the event, Rosberg joked that he was the man to criticise after a race heavily criticised for its lack of action.

But Sainz pushed back.

According to him, the circuit had already been designed and approved by the FIA before he signed his ambassador agreement. He even admitted being frustrated that he had not been given the opportunity to contribute to the layout.

Sainz may have been one of the public faces of the Madrid Grand Prix, but being its ambassador does not make him its circuit designer.

Was Rosberg’s criticism fair, or was Sainz simply the easiest person to blame?

🎙️ Nico Rosberg via Sky Sports F1
🎙️ Carlos Sainz via Nextgen-Auto

#F1 #Formula1 #CarlosSainz #NicoRosberg #MadridGP #Madring #SpanishGP

While Max Verstappen tried to present the incident as Hamilton almost taking him out of the race, Laurent Mekies gave a much simpler and more realistic explanation.

Red Bull believed that keeping the positions would inevitably have resulted in a five or ten-second penalty.

That is why the team asked Max to let both Antonelli and Hamilton back through — despite knowing Hamilton was already experiencing a problem and could potentially retire.

Mekies also understood something Max’s radio messages ignored: a time penalty can cost far more than the positions surrendered on track, especially if a Safety Car changes the race later.

So Red Bull did not ask Verstappen to give the place back because they suddenly stopped supporting their driver.

They did it because they knew the position was not defensible.

Hamilton had made the better start and got ahead. Max avoided contact by using the run-off, but then rejoined in front. Avoiding an accident was sensible; retaining the advantage gained off-track was not.

Max supplied the emotion and attempted to control the narrative.

Mekies supplied the sporting reality.

And his explanation indirectly confirms what Red Bull already understood during the race: returning the position was not “Mickey Mouse racing”. It was the only sensible way to avoid an inevitable penalty.

Do Mekies’ comments settle the debate over the incident?

Quote: F1 TV via Formula1.com
📸 Formula 1 / PlanetF1

#F1 #LaurentMekies #MaxVerstappen #LewisHamilton #RedBullRacing #SpanishGP

CARLOS SAINZ THINKS FERNANDO ALONSO TALKED HIM INTO A PENALTY. 👀

On Lap 14 in Madrid, Alonso closed on Sainz approaching Turn 5. The two Spaniards made contact, damaging Alonso’s front wing.

The stewards concluded that Sainz moved towards the right-hand edge after the deceleration phase had already begun and should have left more room. The usual sanction for moving under braking would have been a black-and-white flag, but the contact turned it into a five-second penalty.

Sainz saw the incident very differently.

He argued that there was only room for one car through the right-left sequence, that he could not continuously watch his mirrors while negotiating the corner and that Alonso was not properly alongside.

But his strongest accusation concerned Fernando’s radio message: Sainz believes Alonso’s complaints helped influence the outcome.

That is the bigger debate.

Drivers know that team radio is no longer only communication with their engineers. It can also frame an incident in real time for Race Control, the broadcasters and millions of spectators.

However, the stewards stated that their verdict was based on video, telemetry and onboard footage.

Did Alonso’s radio influence the penalty — or did the evidence make it inevitable?

📸 Formula 1 / F1 TV

#F1 #Formula1 #CarlosSainz #FernandoAlonso #SpanishGP #Madring #WilliamsF1 #AstonMartinF1 #F1Interviews

“HE HAS TO BE SUCCESSFUL — THEN HE LEAVES WHENEVER HE WANTS.”

FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem believes Fernando Alonso should not leave Formula 1 because Aston Martin and Honda are currently uncompetitive.

Speaking in Madrid, he said it was “not acceptable” for a two-time World Champion to arrive in his own country and find himself at the back of the grid.

But when did the FIA’s role include ensuring that a particular driver must be successful before retiring?

The FIA can create neutral mechanisms such as ADUO, allowing any engine manufacturer that meets the performance-deficit criteria to spend more and introduce additional upgrades.

What it should not do is make competitive success sound like something a champion is personally entitled to receive.

Alonso subsequently said he had not spoken to Ben Sulayem about this. His weekly conversations are with Stefano Domenicali — and his message is not simply that Aston Martin needs a faster car.

His message is that Formula 1 itself cannot continue like this.

Should the FIA help write the ending to a champion’s career — or simply guarantee fair competition for everyone?

Source: RacingNews365 / New Economy Forum, Madrid

#F1 #FernandoAlonso #BenSulayem #FIA #AstonMartin

HAAS ARE TESTING THE FUTURE. OCON HAS JUST POINTED AT THE PRESENT.

With no confirmation for 2027, every Haas test involving another driver inevitably increases the pressure on Esteban Ocon.

The team recently ran Ryo Hirakawa, Leonardo Fornaroli and Rafael Câmara at Portimão — three names that can only fuel speculation surrounding his seat.

Ocon’s response was calm, but unmistakably defensive: when the VF-26 behaves as expected, he believes both sides of the garage deliver.

In other words, changing the driver would not solve what he sees as Haas’ real weakness: an inconsistent car.

But the pressure is not invented. Bearman leads their qualifying head-to-head 12–6 and the points standings 18–3. At the same time, Haas have now gone seven consecutive races without scoring, suggesting the problem is clearly bigger than one driver.

This feels like more than a defence of Ocon’s season. It also sounds like a warning to Haas:

Before evaluating replacements, make sure you have properly evaluated the car.

Is Ocon right — or is he deflecting the pressure surrounding his 2027 seat?

#F1 #EstebanOcon #HaasF1 #SpanishGP

Nico Rosberg has just said exactly what I recently argued about Andrea Stella and McLaren.

Lando Norris is 55 points ahead of Oscar Piastri, has been in stronger form and remains McLaren’s only remotely realistic Drivers’ Championship contender.

Yet McLaren continues to treat permanent neutrality as an absolute principle.

At Monza, Stella explained that both drivers had the same car, the same tyres and the same tyre age, so McLaren decided to let them race. That may sound fair when looking at one isolated battle. But over an entire championship, equal treatment is not always the best sporting strategy.

If one driver has the points, the form and the momentum, the team must recognise that reality and maximise its strongest opportunity.

This is not about disrespecting Oscar. It is about Andrea Stella understanding that refusing to choose is still a decision — and one that has too often ended up benefiting Piastri.

Rosberg even suggested that contractual clauses may prevent McLaren from officially treating Oscar as a number two. But the sporting question remains:

At what point does McLaren stop protecting the appearance of equality and start supporting the driver who is currently giving them their best chance?

#F1 #NicoRosberg #LandoNorris #OscarPiastri #AndreaStella #McLaren #ItalianGP

Fred Vasseur has made his preference clear: he wants to let Hamilton and Leclerc race for as long as possible.

That position is understandable. No team principal wants to freeze positions unnecessarily, create tension between his drivers or establish a hierarchy before it becomes essential.

But Ferrari may now have waited so long that Vasseur will never actually have to make that difficult decision.

Why?

Because, from my point of view, the championship opportunity has already disappeared.

Ferrari needed to maximise Hamilton’s points when he was their closest driver to the championship leaders — particularly during a period in which the car was no longer regularly capable of fighting for victories or pole positions.

Instead, the team continued postponing the decision.

Points were potentially left on the table in Hungary. Ferrari failed to maximise its result in Zandvoort. Then came Monza, where the absence of clear rules contributed to another disastrous outcome for the team.

Vasseur wanted to preserve freedom between his drivers until a decision became unavoidable.

But timing is everything in a championship fight.

If you wait until the mathematical situation forces you to establish a hierarchy, you may already have missed the period during which that hierarchy could have made a difference.

In the end, Vasseur may get exactly what he wanted: no team orders between Hamilton and Leclerc.

Not because Ferrari found the perfect balance — but because it is now too late for those orders to change the championship.

Was Vasseur right to remain neutral, or did Ferrari simply wait too long?

Vasseur : “For a team, it's never good to lose points. This is clear. Now, basically at the beginning of the season, I think every single team principal in the world would love to let them race. “To freeze positions when you are the team principal, don't imagine that it's an easy choice. You do it for the team, you do it for the results at the end, but it's never an easy call.” “By definition, I would love to let them race all the weekend. Now, by reason, you have to take a decision at one stage,” “Each team is different. We will have to take a decision when we'll decide.”

George Russell’s explanation for why the early stages of the Italian Grand Prix remained so closely contested is that nobody could break the slipstream.

Every time a driver moved into the lead, they became vulnerable to being overtaken again. According to Russell, this allowed the cars behind to remain attached to the leading group.

That may explain why Russell struggled to create a gap and lost time while fighting at the front. But does it really explain why he was beaten by Antonelli?

Russell started second. Antonelli started 19th and still had to navigate traffic, complete numerous overtakes, catch the leaders and then win the race.

The slipstream may have kept the field together, but Antonelli did not have an easier race. If anything, Russell’s explanation makes his teammate’s performance look even more impressive.

Is this fair context from Russell — or an excuse for losing to Antonelli despite starting 17 places ahead?

#F1 #Formula1 #GeorgeRussell #KimiAntonelli #MercedesF1 #ItalianGP

Is this genuine praise for Carlos Sainz — or is Williams trying to justify the driver it has just extended?

James Vowles has described Sainz as the best driver he has worked with when it comes to interacting with engineers. Asked whether that included Lewis Hamilton, he answered: “More than Lewis in that respect, yes.”

To be clear, Vowles is not saying that Sainz is a better overall driver than Hamilton. He is highlighting one specific quality: Carlos’ ability to connect what he feels inside the car with the precise data point that explains it.

That may be a completely genuine assessment. But the timing is interesting.

Williams recently gave Sainz a new multi-year contract despite a disastrous 2026 season. The team is ninth in the Constructors’ Championship and Sainz has scored only six points. Presenting him as an exceptional technical leader helps justify the extension and reassures everyone that progress is happening behind the scenes.

But it also raises an unavoidable question.

If Sainz is capable of transforming a team from within, why could Ferrari not win a championship during his four seasons there? And why is Williams still so far away after almost two years with him?

A driver’s feedback is valuable, but it is still only one input. He does not design the aerodynamic concept, control correlation, manufacture the upgrades or make every strategic decision.

Ferrari actually came within 14 points of winning the 2024 Constructors’ Championship, so Sainz clearly contributed to a competitive team. But Williams’ current position shows that even outstanding feedback cannot repair an entire organisation by itself.

So yes, I believe Vowles probably means what he says.

But publicly comparing Sainz favourably with Hamilton also flatters Carlos, validates Vowles’ recruitment decision and shifts attention away from the performance of the car.

Genuine praise and strategic communication can both be true at the same time.

#F1 #CarlosSainz #JamesVowles #WilliamsF1 #LewisHamilton #Formula1

Fernando Alonso has just said out loud what Monza made impossible to ignore in 2026.

At the “Temple of Speed”, his Aston Martin reached around 312km/h — below the figures he experienced at Barcelona and Budapest.

For me, this is an open criticism of the new regulations.

Of course, Aston Martin’s Honda power deficit amplified Alonso’s figure. But this is bigger than one car.

In 2025, Monza recorded the highest peak speed of the entire season at 365km/h. In 2026, it dropped to fifth place, while Barcelona led the ranking at 360km/h.

That is the paradox of these cars: on the longest straights, the electrical deployment fades earlier. The cars can stop accelerating — or even begin losing speed — before reaching the braking zone.

F1 can argue that the new formula is more efficient and technologically sophisticated. But if Monza no longer showcases ultimate straight-line speed, then the regulations have removed part of what makes each circuit unique.

Lap time alone does not define the spectacle. The way the cars produce that lap matters too.

Do you agree with Alonso? Have the 2026 regulations taken the “speed” out of the Temple of Speed?

Source: Fernando Alonso via F1i.com
